1. FROM MY DESK
The world's richest people are embracing a new form of philanthropy: giving a couple hundred dollars to children, one investment account at a time.

Elon Musk is pledging (SpaceX) shares to millions of kids, joining Michael Dell and other billionaires in seeding the new Trump Accounts program. The effort comes as Silicon Valley titans are increasingly cast as societal villains. Communities across the country are opposing data centers, and some polling shows many Americans say they want billionaires to have less political, economic and cultural power.

The payouts idea came from tech investor Brad Gerstner, who sold the concept to the White House and envisions it as a new social contract between the wealthiest Americans and the rest of society. Critics see a political stunt packed with tax advantages for the ultrarich. Erich Schwartzel and Konrad Putzier explore whether these giveaways can keep the pitchforks at bay.

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you're not subscribed, sign up here. If you're reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.
2. TODAY'S HEADLINES
House Democrats are targeting Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, weighing impeachment as one of their first moves if they take back the House in the midterms.
A wave of AI-powered attacks has hit the internet in recent weeks, as hackers armed with agents and other tools make intrusions faster and far harder to trace.

The yellow-vest protest movement paralyzed Paris eight years ago. Now it is re-emerging as part of a coalition across France demanding solutions to the high cost of living and other economic complaints.
Ukraine said its Starlink system was working normally again, raising hopes of an end to the dayslong disruption to the vital satellite internet service by Elon Musk's SpaceX was ending.
An Anduril-backed startup is genetically engineering military dogs to run faster, have a keener sense of smell and avoid inherited diseases.
Our national security correspondent got rare access to a U.S. aircraft carrier conducting missions in the Strait of Hormuz, as it prepares for potential strikes on Iranian targets.
3. FROM THE MARKETS

To the scientific world, Moderna's cancer vaccine's results proved that a highly personalized, immune-targeting medication can work. To investors, it didn't work well enough, with shares tanking. Columnist David Wainer writes that even after the sharp fall, the drugmaker's stock assumes wild successes.
4. READ IT HERE FIRST
Government grift emerges as a defining midterm issue.

Less than two weeks before the midterms, corruption is suddenly eclipsing inflation as voters' top concern. A string of damaging headlines about the president's inner circle-ranging from a longtime adviser facing a Justice Department inquiry, to a Russian businessman funding his son's lavish wedding afterparty-has left Republican operatives wringing their hands. With Democrats hammering the issue in ads, strategists worry these self-dealing allegations could make a challenging election even harder. Our reporters break down the growing anxiety, and why the fallout could cost Republicans at the ballot box.
The secret playbook behind A24's Elizabeth Holmes smash hit.

For nearly three years, indie studio A24 pulled off a minor Hollywood miracle: keeping its Elizabeth Holmes documentary a complete secret-even from most of its employees. Fewer than 10 staffers knew directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim had embedded with the convicted Theranos fraudster just weeks before she reported to federal prison. That secrecy eventually became the film's most potent marketing weapon. "You Can See Everything" scored a $15 million box-office debut-the biggest for a non-music documentary since 2004. John Jurgensen and Ben Fritz reveal how the studio turned a stealth production into a massive cultural phenomenon.

6. SEE THE STORY
You were once smarter than AI at math. Yes, even you.

Five years ago, frontier AI models could barely pass a basic arithmetic test. Today, those same systems have graduated from grade-school homework to solving open research problems that eluded humans for decades. Columnist Ben Cohen looks at how AI went from failing simple math to transforming the field forever. Can you beat the early AI models? Take the quiz.
7. HAPPENING THIS WEEKEND

Saturday: Protests are planned across France, with yellow-vest demonstrators, students and labor unions expected to participate. The Tampa Bay Rays face the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 2 of the World Series.

Sunday: Brazil holds a closely contested presidential runoff between incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro. The NFL stages its first regular-season game in Paris, despite the protests.

8. THE NUMBER

That is the median age for becoming a grandmother today, up from 44 in 1960. Because Americans are waiting longer to have children, this demographic shift is shrinking the healthy years grandparents get to spend actively involved with their grandkids from 28 years down to just 15. But there is a silver lining: Older, retired people are more likely to have time to be with grandchildren, and spending on each grandchild grows as family sizes shrink.
9. AND FINALLY...
The biggest No. 1 in Billboard history is one you might not have heard.

Ella Langley's country hit "Choosin' Texas" recently broke a Billboard Hot 100 record by spending 24 weeks in the top spot, dethroning Mariah Carey. With attention split across a million platforms and highly personalized TikTok algorithms, old mainstream unifiers like radio and TV have lost much of their power. And because the hit didn't top the streaming charts in markets like New York and Los Angeles, it shows how a massive multiweek No. 1 can easily pass people by when media is no longer centralized.
